With perhaps the most important election day in American history looming mere weeks from now, a new threat is changing the traditional calculus of climate change politics between Democrats and Republicans – the headlong rush among tech giants to build massive data centre for their AI development. 
Grassroots communities in almost every US state are rising up to protest the sudden planning and construction of these massive complexes, arguing that their unquantified use of electric power, as well as local water supplies to cool their systems is a devastating environmental threat. What bothers the locals in particular is the secrecy behind the projects, which only adds to rising suspicious about AI. 
Coming after a summer of extreme heat, wildfires, storms, and floods – capped by the deadly disaster in Nepal last month – the issue is being taken seriously by both parties. Candidates are staking out positions as hundreds of moratoriums on new construction are passed throughout the country. 





“Maybe data centers are what unites us all after all,” said Erin Brockovich, the famous environmental advocate who is leading a campaign to map all the data centers, in an interview last week with The Independent.
As of mid-2026, more than 4,000 data centres were currently operational in the U.S., with as many as 1,500 new ones in the planning and construction phase, according to the Pew Research Center. In the global AI arms race to be the first to develop superhuman intelligence, giant companies such as Meta, Google, Amazon, SpaceX, Anthropic, and Open AI are rushing to build out capacity, urged on by President Donald Trump to beat China to the punch.

articles.jina_text:
The accelerating climate crisis and this year’s record-breaking El Niño mean that, although the summer’s heatwaves are still fresh in the memory, households in the UK are already being told to prepare for a potentially destructive winter of storms and heavy rain – leaving millions of homes at risk of flooding.
Government action is needed to improve flood defences and build reliance on a national and regional level. But with the UK’s flood season just weeks away, the Guardian spoke to experts to find out what action communities and individuals can take to make their neighbourhoods and homes more resilient, from self-closing airbricks to deflated children’s footballs.

Community action
The first step is to check whether your home or neighbourhood is listed at risk of flooding on the government’s website. If it is, find out if the local council has a flood alert scheme and make sure you and your neighbours are signed up to that and the Environment Agency’s flood alerts system.
Join any local community flood group – or consider setting one up with neighbours – and approach the council to see what flood plans it has in place, and get involved in making them better. This could include lobbying for more permeable surfaces, rain gardens and tree planting.


Identify any vulnerable residents who might need extra support and draw up a street or neighbourhood flood plan to make sure everyone knows what to do in the event of a flood.
Tracey Garrett, the chief executive of the National Flood Forum, said flooding can be “incredibly frightening and disruptive” but insists that together, communities, households and councils can make difference to an area’s resilience.
“We are seeing increasingly intense rainfall and a growing risk from surface water flooding, and climate change means we cannot assume that the flooding patterns of the past will necessarily be the patterns of the future,” she said. “This makes preparation more important than ever.”
Gardens and outdoor spaces
According to Mary Long-Dhonau, who runs the Flood Mary campaign, protecting your home starts outside. She says now is an ideal time to check brickwork and mortar on outside walls for cracks or weaknesses. These should either be repaired or replaced and external walls can be treated with a breathable waterproof sealant.
“Having cracks or crumbling mortar can be like having 20 taps in your wall that will let the flood water straight in,” said Long-Dhonau, who provides a directory of builders who specialise in flood-related work.


Experts also suggest making sure gutters are clear and in good working order. Long-Dhonau adds that residents should consider installing water butts, which catch and store the rain before it reaches the ground. “They are easy and relatively cheap and it means if you get a warning about a possible flood risk you can empty the water butts before the rain arrives, meaning they have full capacity to hold the maximum amount once the rain starts, keeping it out of the drains

Burning forests, emptying rivers, €180bn in damage: Europe’s politicians face reckoning after ‘summer of truth’ 


Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?




It was, according to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the “summer of truth”. Climate chaos ripped through Europe and the northern hemisphere, sending heat records tumbling, scorching crops in the fields, burning forests, emptying rivers and reservoirs, warping train tracks, melting roads and killing about 35,000 people in Europe alone.
The EU has estimated the damage at about €180bn, and the full bill is yet to arrive: harvests have been depleted, which will probably raise food price inflation, and expensive repairs to infrastructure have only just begun.

“All of this is a mere preview,” said von der Leyen in her state of the EU address on Wednesday. “These were the hottest summer months ever – but probably the coolest of the years to come. Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate targets.”


View image in fullscreen
Streets were flooded in Bangladesh this summer as extreme rainfall fell across Asia. Photograph: Monirul Alam/EPA
But while Europe has heated faster than any other continent, no region of the world is being spared. In the US, this summer’s heat eclipsed that of the “dust bowl” years of the 1930s, and drought gripped 60% of the country from spring, a record for the time of year. Extreme rainfall across Asia brought flash floods and typhoons, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and causing severe damage to crops.


So what has the political response been? Tepid at best from centrist and leftwing politicians, say campaigners, with few rays of hope to brighten the gloom; denial and dangerous, provocative incoherence from the right and far right.
“It was the hottest of summers – it was the meekest of responses,” said Magda Stoczkiewicz, the EU programme director for Greenpeace, of von der Leyen’s intervention. “The EU Commission continues its crusade to dismantle and defund environmental action. It is planning to cut green funding in the next EU budget, continues to support fossil fuels like gas, and is speeding up permitting of environmentally harmful projects.”

At Reform UK’s party conference earlier this month, the party’s chair Lee Anderson MP said in a Q&A session: “What we don’t want to see on farmers’ land is solar panels up and down the country. There’s literally thousands of square miles on farmland.”




This figure is not correct, and in fact it’s a substantial overstatement. Most land used for solar farms was previously agricultural land, but the total area of land estimated to be covered by them is much less than “thousands of square miles”.








In September 2024, ground-mounted solar panels covered “an estimated 21,200 hectares (52,000 acres)” or “around 0.1 per cent of the total land area of the UK”, according to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ).




21,200 hectares is equivalent to approximately 81.9 square miles, or about 0.1% of the total UK land area of 24,438,000 hectares.




The DESNZ told Full Fact this remains its latest estimate.




Last year researchers at Lancaster University produced a slightly lower estimate of up to 17,364 hectares, or 67 square miles. They estimated that of this, around 10,118 hectares (39 square miles) may have previously been arable or horticulture land.




We contacted Mr Anderson for comment.




The amount of land used for solar is expected to increase in the coming years. The government’s UK Solar Roadmap sets out that “up to 0.4% of total UK land” could be required for solar by 2030, while other projections put potential land use as even higher. But even the largest future estimates we’ve seen are less than the “thousands of square miles” referred to by Mr Anderson.













London’s white population has not ‘plummeted to 34%’




Posts shared on social media have claimed that the white population in London has dropped to 34%. But that isn’t correct, according to the latest census data.




That data, which was recorded in 2021, shows that at the time 53.8%, not 34%, of people in London identified as white.









This includes 36.8% who identified as “White: English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British”, plus a further 17% recorded as “White: Other”, which includes those who said they were white Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, Roma or any other white background.




We’ve not found any more recent data reliably recording the ethnicity of London’s population, and no other credible evidence to support the 34% claim.

Australia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cards

Adam Morton






Credits are treated as a straight alternative to emissions cuts, but carbon stored in nature is different to burning millennia-old fossil fuels





The fight within the Greens that led senators to cross the floor last week over koala protection in a national park may have finally put a spotlight on a bigger issue – one at the heart of much of Australia’s promise to act on the climate crisis. It’s this: the country and its polluting industries are too reliant on carbon offsets. The more reliance is placed on them, the more they look like a house of cards.
Offsets can be a mind-deadening subject, but they matter. In Australia, they are known as Australian Carbon Credit Units. Each credit is said to represent one tonne of greenhouse gas that isn’t in the atmosphere and otherwise would have been. They are mostly generated from government-sanctioned projects that are meant to regenerate forests or capture and burn methane released from landfill sites.

These type of projects have plenty to recommend them. With global heating moving into increasingly dangerous territory, the world needs to retain and regenerate all the forests it can, and create new ones. It also needs to sharply reduce how much methane and carbon dioxide is poured into the atmosphere.
But we need to be realistic about what these carbon credits can and can’t do.
Australian carbon credits are treated as a like-for-like alternative for emissions cuts by fossil fuel producers, factories and other big polluting sites. Under the climate policy applied to big industrial facilities responsible for about a third of national pollution – the safeguard mechanism – there is no requirement that businesses make direct emissions cuts. They can just buy an unlimited number of offsets and claim them as their own reductions.


This flexibility makes life easier for the owners of industrial sites that, under changes introduced by Labor three years ago, need to cut emissions intensity – the amount of pollution pumped out per unit of production – by between 1% and 4.9% a year. But it also creates problems.
Geologically stored carbon that is dug up and used as coal, gas or oil has been underground for millennia. When it is brought to the surface and set on fire it releases heat-trapping gas that otherwise couldn’t escape. That gas can persist in the atmosphere for thousands of years.

Clutching surfboards clad with slogans like “end sewage pollution” in gaffer tape, Giles Bristow – chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage – and a group of campaigners delivered their petition signed by 350,000 people to number 10 Downing Street earlier this month. Their message was simple: clean up Britain’s polluted water.
The charity has been campaigning on the issue for its entire 36-year existence. But this year, it's been thrust into the country's consciousness amid the extreme droughts and floods which have laid bare the extent of the issue – as well as through Channel 4's incredibly powerful and must-watch docu-drama, Dirty Business which the charity worked on. 
Dirty Business portrayed the story of Heather Preen, an eight-year-old girl who died in 1999 after contracting E. coli 0157 (the most dangerous strain) during a family holiday in Devon, following a sewage spill. Heather’s mother, Julie Maughan, has continued campaigning for cleaner water with the charity ever since and was also at Downing Street.

Recommended

The Climate 100 List: Engineer Joseph Nguthiru on turning the world’s most invasive plant into bioplastic
The petition is calling to “clean up” the government's proposed Clean Water Bill, and to end the broken privatised ownership of our water system that's been in place since 1989 that "pollutes for profit" and does "not prioritise the environment or our health," Bristow tells me when we meet at Surfers Against Sewage’s offices in St Agnes, Cornwall. 





Surfers Against Sewage is creating a groundswell for systemic change, with Bristow saying that for the majority of businesses "the only duty that exists is to return a reasonable profit to shareholders".





Andy Burnham cannot ignore this tidal wave of public opinion. This is just the tip of the iceberg of the people who care about this issue
The number of signatures show the public is increasingly unwilling to accept polluted rivers and seas as normal. "We're firmly putting this on [prime minister] Andy Burnham's agenda – he cannot ignore this tidal wave of public opinion. This is just the tip of the iceberg of the people who care about this issue,” Bristow says.


This summer has also made the issue even more difficult to ignore. During July and August, Surfers Against Sewage recorded more than 43,000 hours of sewage discharges into England’s waters, including more than 2,000 hours into designated bathing waters. Water companies are only permitted to discharge untreated sewage only following heavy rainfall and storms, when the systems are overloaded – yet it's been the hottest summer on record, with barely any rainfall.

More than 1,600 critically imperiled species protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA) face losing further federal protections following a new reinterpretation of the 1973 law by the Donald Trump administration.
A September 14 memo distributed to Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) field offices by FWS director Brian Nesvik calls for a reinterpretation of what it means to “take” an endangered species. Under the ESA, “take” is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct”.

The memo, obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, reinterprets the law to mean that harming or killing an endangered animal would no longer be considered illegal unless the action was specifically intended to cause harm or death.



“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” the memo said, adding: “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”
The reinterpretation effectively excludes economic activities such as logging, mining and industrial development from the ESA’s prohibition on “take” when those activities foreseeably kill or injure wildlife without intentionally targeting them.
The memo follows the Trump administration’s repeal in July of the ESA’s definition of prohibited “harm,” which was defined as “an act which actually kills or injures wildlife,” including acts that “may include significant habitat modification or degradation”.
Interior secretary Doug Burgum justified the repeal in July by saying: “For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.”
Earlier this month, 20 states and Washington DC sued the Trump administration over its decision to redefine “harm,” including removing “modification or degradation” of habitat from conduct that can constitute a prohibited take.


In a statement on Thursday to the Guardian about the administration’s reinterpretation of “take,” the interior department, which oversees the FWS, said: “As outlined in the final rule, the department determined that the previous regulatory definition of ‘harm’ expanded the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on ‘take’ beyond the text Congress enacted. As well as at least 1,300 people who are known to have been killed, more than 5,000 are missing, some of them trapped in tunnels linked to the 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the floods. The first academic study linking the disaster to the climate crisis will now be added to that application. Scientists at Imperial College London, along with international collaborators on the World Weather Attribution project, found that a number of drivers of the glacier fall had been made worse by atmospheric heating. Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue 
 
 
British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it 
 
UK politics live – latest updates 




The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate.
Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK.







British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it 
Andy Burnham


Read more
The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues.
“I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.”
Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.”


He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead.
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.”
The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.
A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency.
A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdaw has been delayed until later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profile Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer.


Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off.

After losing much of its forests in recent decades, ordinary citizens have led the way in planting saplings across the country as part of the government’s Green Legacy Initiative




When Halima Kedir first began planting trees, she was met with scepticism and even mockery. “My neighbours discouraged me,” she recalls, sitting on a wooden chair in her garden, which is lush with the trees and fruits she has planted – banana, olive and grevillea among them.
“They thought I was striving for nothing, but with time, many are realising that trees can be part of the solution to our problems as a way to fight climate change and food insecurity,” she says.

Kedir, 35, who lives in the Berbere district of Ethiopia’s Oromia region, became an accidental environmentalist after planting thousands of trees – she has lost count of how many – inspiring others to follow suit.
In a nation with a history of large-scale deforestation, Kedir’s work has not been easy. It has required moral courage and practical endurance. As her trees took root and her surroundings became greener, the people who doubted began to respect what she was doing, she says. “Now, everything has changed. Those who tried to dissuade me are envious of my effort and commitment.”
For Kedir, trees are more than just plants, they are living companions and part of a solution to some of the challenges her community faces in one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable nations.
From the turn of the century to 2025, Ethiopia lost 560,000 hectares (2,160 sq miles) of its tree cover, due to the expansion of agriculture, commercial logging and the use of charcoal as fuel. This has resulted in devastating impacts on biodiversity, soil quality and water resources as well as increasing the risk of climate-related disasters.
But thanks to a number of initiatives introduced by the Ethiopian government, including a massive tree-planting scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative (GLI) in 2019, the rate of deforestation has slowed. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from 92,000 hectares to 27,703 hectares. Meanwhile, forest cover has increased from 15.5% to 23.6% during the same period.
Through the GLI, the government claims to have planted 48bn trees in seven years, including a reported record-breaking 353m seedlings in one day. Its goal is to plant 50bn trees by 2030.

There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Dr Friederike Otto, an Imperial College London climatologist who co-authored the study.
Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing.
Scientists say the floods were caused by a collapse of rock wall and glacier ice near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.
The study said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses














According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (2.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate".
Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability.
Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year.
Climate change, while not the only cause of the disaster, was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", the study said.
In the wake of the floods, Nepal's leaders have said the country needs around $5bn (£3.7bn) to rebuild itself.
The UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which came into operation last year, requires countries to submit evidence proving that the losses they faced were caused by climate change.
Nepali officials had been preparing satellite and drone images, as well as preliminary reports, to back up its request to the fund.
But the World Weather Attribution report is now the strongest evidence for their claim that climate change was a significant factor in the collapse of rock and ice at Langtang Lirung, authorities say.





The report "will be the main basis of our claim as it has detailed what role climate has played in this disaster," said Maheshwar Dhakal, spokesperson for Nepal's Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.

articles.jina_text:
Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.
Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.








How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide

Read more
“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.
“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”


View image in fullscreen
A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.
It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.
“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”
The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.
Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

Climate Change Committee says government cannot expand airport without requiring aviation industry to clean up its emissions 




Heathrow airport should be allowed to expand only if airlines pay for the removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the government’s climate advisers have said.
Building a third runway and new terminals, as some in government want to do, would breach the UK’s carbon budgets and make reaching net zero by 2050 impossible, on current policies, according to the Climate Change Committee.

The “only way” to manage such expansion within the UK’s climate commitments was for the aviation industry to become more efficient, use an increasing proportion of “sustainable aviation fuels” (SAF) in place of fossil fuels, and pay for the permanent removal and storage of carbon from the atmosphere.


Nigel Topping, the chair of the CCC, said: “The government cannot expand Heathrow airport without requiring the aviation industry to clean up its emissions. Therefore, the government should legislate policies that require the aviation industry to fully address all of their emissions by 2050, either directly or by purchasing engineered removals. The polluter-pays principle must apply.”
In a report to the government on Wednesday, the CCC found that the costs of SAF and carbon removal would probably be passed on to passengers by airlines, adding an estimated £150 to the price of a return flight to Alicante by 2050, or about £400 to the price of a flight to New York. These costs would be phased in gradually over 25 years.
But campaigners rejected the CCC’s plan of relying on nascent technologies to wipe out the impact of an expansion that would commit the UK to much higher emissions for decades, and called on ministers to halt all airport expansion.
Tony Bosworth, campaigner at Friends of the Earth, accused the CCC of “pulling its punches”, pointing to recent research by the Tyndall Centre that found SAF and carbon removals were unproven and unlikely to ramp up in time to the extent needed to justify airport expansion.


“The CCC should have made it crystal clear: there is no plausible way to expand Heathrow without wrecking the UK’s climate targets,” he said.
Frequent flying is overwhelming skewed towards the wealthy. In any year, only about half of people in England take a flight abroad, while about 80% of all flights abroad were taken by people who took two or more flights – about a quarter of the population. Those in the highest income group took 38% of all flights abroad – four times as many flights as those in the lowest income group, according to the National Travel Survey of England in 2024.

Bristol has become the first British city to impose a ban on the advertising of fast fashion, in new restrictions that will also curb ads for SUVs and airlines.
The ban is part of moves by the West Country city, known for its radical political scene, to impose sweeping bans on advertising for polluting industries.

Restrictions have also been placed on advertising SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on advertising sites owned by the Green-run council.
“We don’t want Bristol to be a billboard for polluters while we’re working hard to improve health, air quality and nature in the city,” said Heather Mack, Bristol city council’s deputy leader.
“We’re proud to be thinking holistically about the changes we need to keep Bristol green and thriving.”


Bristol council’s strategy and resources committee passed the new advertising and sponsorship policy by an eight to one vote on Monday. It updates a policy passed in 2021 which made Bristol the first council outside London to ban junk food ads.

Firms manage $7.3tn in assets and could afford to transition away from fossil fuels yet invest in natural gas and coal-fired plants to power datacenters




The energy portfolios of 20 private equity firms produce 1.5bn tons of greenhouse gases a year, more than the annual emissions of any country except China, the US, India and Russia, according to a new report.
Together, these firms manage $7.3tn in assets of all kinds, affording them the ability to shape the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels. However their energy investments include significant fossil fuel assets including natural gas and coal-fired power plants to provide electricity to datacenters.

The analysis of the top 20 private equity firms invested in global energy infrastructure was conducted by the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. It found that the firms owned 15,000 miles of pipelines, 124GW of power generation capacity across 370 fossil fuel-powered plants and hundreds of oil and gas fields.


Half of the top 10 US datacenter owners are backed by private equity, said Matt Parr, the communications director for Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), one of the organizations in the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. “This industry doesn’t get enough scrutiny and credit for its contribution to global emissions,” Parr said. “It’s a very opaque business model.”
The research team queried energy holdings with the private markets data provider PitchBook, drawing on additional details from company websites, press releases, news articles and regulatory filings. Because of gaps in the data, the researchers were unable to calculate how much the 20 private equity firms invested in fossil fuel assets. But an earlier analysis of data compiled on PitchBook shows that private equity has funded more than $1tn in fossil fuel assets since 2010, said Amanda Mendoza, senior research and campaign coordinator on the climate team at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project.
While some public-sector retirement systems have been trying to limit their exposure to fossil fuel projects, the private equity firms BlackRock, GIP, Energy Capital Partners, EQT and Kayne Anderson increased the amount of fossil fuel companies in their portfolio compared with 2024, according to the report.


The private equity firm EQT has positioned itself as a climate conscious investor, supporting the energy transition. But EQT, along with Blackrock’s GIP and the California Public Employees’ Retirement system could soon acquire AES Corporation, which owns more than 20 power plants. “It is alarming because if this deal does go through they will then be owners of a fleet of coal power and gas powered plants,” Mendoza said. “That’s significantly going to impact their transition. It seems like they’re transitioning to fossil fuels instead of away.”

A less visible but still menacing casualty of climate change and human misuse is the fall in the water level of the Spey and the vast network of tributaries which feed it. Scrap windfall tax on oil and gas firms early, North Sea industry urges


Labour should replace levy in 2027 rather than 2030 as energy bills are poised to surge over the winter, says lobby group




The North Sea oil and gas industry has called on Labour to scrap the windfall tax on fossil fuel firms three years early, as Britain heads into a winter with energy bills expected to reach their highest level since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), the industry’s trade body, wants the tax replaced in 2027, rather than in 2030, with a narrower levy that only applies during price spikes.

OEUK is also pressing ministers to approve two big North Sea oil and gasfields, Rosebank and Jackdaw, as part of a call for looser regulation of the sector.

The current windfall tax, the energy profits levy, was introduced in 2022 after fossil fuel firms posted record profits when oil and gas prices spiked after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Its planned replacement, the oil and gas revenue levy, would charge a 35% tax on revenue only when prices rise above a set threshold.
Any decision to ease taxes on oil and gas producers would come before what is likely to be another winter of high energy prices due to the Iran war. Household energy bills are expected to climb to a three-year high this winter, while wholesale gas on Monday rose to 207p a therm, its highest point since the Russia-Ukraine crisis.
Companies including Shell and BP have already enjoyed huge profits in the months after the Iran war, which the campaign group Global Witness described as “cashing in on human misery”.


The OEUK chief executive, David Whitehouse, admitted that “from the consumer’s point of view … you can argue that it is a difficult time to make these arguments”.
However, he added that the new levy would “ensure that oil and gas companies pay high levels of tax when prices are high, but encourages investment”.
“The government talks about the need for resilience, the need to support communities,” he said. “This is a long-term, permanent windfall tax that means fundamentally we pay more tax, not less, and I think that’s important for the UK economy.”
The lobby group says bringing the change forward would prompt up to £50bn of investment in the North Sea and help protect industrial jobs, echoing warnings from some unions about the risks of the transition away from oil and gas for workers.

The ancient craft of hedge laying is experiencing a strong revival as farmers use techniques that peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries to boost wildlife, capture carbon and help tackle flooding.
Hedge laying, which restores and revives mature hedges to keep them fresh, was among the four most popular categories of capital grants selected by farmers out of a total pot of £225m provided by the government this year to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside.

The 2,500 farmers across England who applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using a craft that dates back thousands of years, will – if the grants are approved – lay 1,300km (800 miles) of mature hedgerows, enough to stretch from Land’s End to Hadrian’s Wall and back.

“These grants will give 1,300km of potentially ancient hedges a new lease of life, to help plug the gap, and it is fantastic that it is such a popular grant application.”
Mature, maintained hedgerows are a carbon sink, capturing more carbon in every hectare than forests. They support thousands of species, provide shade for livestock, reduce soil erosion and slow down, absorb and store vast amounts of rainwater to help reduce flooding.
“They are massively important,” said Stephen Budding, the chair of the National Hedgelaying Society. “The greatest biodiversity gain is from hedge laying older hedges.

One of the biggest upheavals in a millennium is on its way, strengthened by the climate crisis. We need leaders who make things better not worse





If you think you have heard enough about the growing “super” El Niño, trust me, you are going to hear a lot more. What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium. It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world in what remains of this year and in 2027, and there is no reason to think the UK will be immune.
To recap briefly, El Niño involves a heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural cycle termed the El Niño southern oscillation, which switches between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases. El Niños that see heating reach or exceed 2C are defined as “super” but this one, which is forecast to top-out at an astonishing 4C later this year, is so much bigger, the term “hyper” might be more appropriate.



El Niño is nothing new. Evidence for its existence extends back hundreds of millions of years and its ramifications have always been negative and disruptive. The difference today is that it is happening at a time when our world is heating more rapidly than ever before, and it is being supercharged as a result, leading to increasingly extreme weather.
Figuring out how much global heating alone is influencing El Niño is not straightforward, as its strength and other characteristics change naturally over time. Both El Niños and La Niñas, for example, have been steadily increasing in duration over the last 7,000 years. This is bad news in its own right, as it means the world’s weather is knocked out of kilter for even longer, but added to this, stronger El Niños are becoming more frequent as we continue to add CO2 to the atmosphere.
There is no straightforward correlation between El Niño’s strength and the magnitude of impacts in any given part of the planet. But given the unprecedented amount of extra heat being added to the atmosphere over the Pacific, it would be reasonable to expect the world to experience exceptionally hazardous weather over the course of the next several months.
How, then, is the UK likely to fare? The Met Office has already warned of the increased likelihood of a stormy and wet autumn and early winter, so it would be judicious to start preparing now for flooding on a serious – perhaps even epic – scale. After all, the last big El Niño, in 2015–16, resulted in the most extreme UK floods on record. Stronger winds are also a big worry, as many trees weakened by this summer’s extreme drought conditions could be brought down in the powerful storms to come. A strong El Niño could also bring Arctic air to the UK later in the winter, although this is far from set in stone. Panama canal traffic to be cut again as drought from El Niño worsens


Latest daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes




The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.
The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.

From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.

The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.


In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.
Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.
The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.
The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.
If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.


In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.

Europe’s summer emergency was a dire warning for Australia. What can be learned before it’s too late?

Nick Rowley





Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined

Back in April 2004, in the shadow of the previous European summer, I started work at Downing Street advising the British prime minister on climate change. The 2003 heatwave had killed an estimated 70,000 people across Europe. Many were older people, in homes and neighbourhoods ill-equipped for prolonged heat.
In May this year, I walked through Bordeaux with my 83-year-old mother-in-law in 38C heat. I saw how quickly heat changes the terms of ordinary life. Streets emptied. Shade became essential. The question was not simply the temperature, but whether people could work, sleep or remain safely at home.

That was the European spring. By summer, 42,000 hectares around Gironde and Arcachon surrounding the city had burned. France experienced its worst fires since 1949.

Read more
In June, during the Tour de Suisse, the Italian champion cyclist Elisa Longo Borghini suffered heatstroke. She struggled afterwards to remember the final climb. If extreme heat can overwhelm an elite athlete, we should understand the danger it presents to us all.
Europe’s warning is relevant to every Australian city.
Extreme heat is not merely uncomfortable weather. Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined. Yet it remains under-recognised because it leaves little visible destruction and its effects are often recorded as heart, kidney or respiratory illness rather than heat itself.
And risk is not evenly shared. Older people, particularly those living alone, people with chronic illness, outdoor workers and people in poorly cooled homes are more exposed. As we age, our ability to sense heat, sweat effectively and regulate body temperature can diminish, while thirst can become a less reliable prompt. Staying hydrated must be a habit throughout a hot day, not an afterthought when work is finished.

articles.jina_text:
Scientists have discovered nine new deep-sea sponge species off Alaska, offering new insights into the region’s largely unexplored marine biodiversity.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) announced the discovery on Thursday, saying the species were found in the Gulf of Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. The findings bring the total number of known sponge species in Alaska to 232.








Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports? 

Read more
The specimens were collected during Noaa Fisheries’ annual bottom-trawl surveys, which monitor groundfish and shellfish stocks. Researchers analyzed samples collected as far back as 2012, describing the new species in two recent scientific papers.
Often described as living water pumps, sponges are among Earth’s earliest multicellular animals, dating back more than 600m years. They filter seawater and help create habitats on the seafloor, despite having no brain or complex organs.
“Sponges are ecologically important,” said Sean Rooney, a Noaa fisheries biologist and co-author of the studies at the agency’s Alaska Fisheries Science Center. “They aren’t plants, but like trees in a forest, they provide complex structure along the seafloor that creates habitat and refuge for commercially important fish and crabs,” he added.
“Each time we find a new species, it opens up new doors … Deep water is hard to access, especially rocky places we can’t reach with bottom-trawl surveys. There are now more than 232 identified species of sponges in Alaska, and probably hundreds more that we don’t know about yet. The future in this field is exciting,” he continued.


View image in fullscreen
Biologists use guides to try to identify species of sponge and fish collected during a bottom-trawl survey. Photograph: Noaa Fisheries
Unlike most marine animals, which can be identified by visible traits such as fins and body shapes, sponges can be much harder to distinguish. Because they lack complex organs and other distinctive external features, scientists often rely on their microscopic skeletons and genetic material to identify them.


“DNA barcodes provide a quick genetic reference,” said Meredith Everett, a biologist at Noaa’s Northwest Fisheries Science Center. “Sponge DNA can be tricky because they filter-feed, and within their tissues we may find foreign DNA and biochemicals that inhibit testing. But despite the challenges, we successfully developed several new barcodes for Alaskan species,” she added.
Dense sponge communities are considered essential fish habitat by Noaa because they provide shelter that supports fish survival, growth and population recovery.
Sponges also produce chemicals to defend themselves against predators and competing organisms. Some of these compounds have shown promise for potential use in cancer treatments.

When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail.
The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations.

I mean climate change is real, I've spent a 25-year career telling people it is real and documenting its impact on the region: Floods, dry spells, heatwaves and more. 
So why for many people does this year feel different - like climate change is finally "here" ?
Well in 2026, things have reached some sort of tipping point where we can start to see really obvious signs of change that had a huge impact on at least some of us.
A winter of endless rain, not just wet but never ending. 
Then the rain stopped and we were hurtling into drought. 
Then wave after wave of what felt like boiling heat.




Image source, West Midlands Fire Service
Image caption, 

Sheldon Country Park was one of the areas in the Midlands left scorched by fire 




We have had wildfires this year because things have been so dry for so long, the hot air has just sucked the moisture out of the landscape.
It leaves vegetation dead, dry and needing just a small spark to erupt into flame.
On Cannock Chase, I spent the day with Staffordshire County Council rangers, as they showed me around the black, scorched earth left behind after the fires that took place there. 
I saw pictures of dead adders along with cracked and burnt eggs belonging to ground-nesting birds.
It is not just wildlife affected by them - the ash from the fire is changing the chemistry of the soil itself. 
It is much more nutrient-rich and that is bad news for this rare lowland heathland, where the traditional plants prefer poorer quality soil.
Already green shoots of bracken are bursting through the blackened earth and that will crowd out the traditional heather, bilberry and cowberry.




Image source, Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service
Image caption, 

At its height, 15 crews tackled a blaze at Sherbrook Valley in Cannock Chase




The Met Office has a list of things climate change will make worse, including "increased risk of fires" but it also says the "habitable region of pests expands".
That is exactly what our farmers are seeing this year.
Bluetongue is an awful disease affecting cattle and sheep, leading to the death of lambs and calves. 
It is carried by infected midges and as the climate has warmed the region, infected midges have expanded north from Europe to now include the Midlands.

articles.jina_text:
Kilos and kilos of courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes and salad leaves are ripe and ready for picking on a small Welsh farm in the rural county of Powys.
The haul being harvested by Tilly Gomersall is not just impressive after a difficult growing season hit by a record string of heatwaves and drought across all of Wales and most of England, but all the more remarkable given that 18 months ago the site was uncultivated pasture.

“Until now, I’ve just been turning the earth with my own power,” Gomersall says. “We’ve got a two-wheel tractor, but you do have to heft that around with your body quite a lot and we’re cultivating from pasture, so it’s really hard work.”
The site at Wern farm, near Newtown, is part of a scheme to encourage young growers to supply fresh produce to nearby towns and cities and boost domestic production in the face of increasing risks to national food supplies.
The 15-hectare (36-acre) site is divided into three plots, each with a holiday chalet where the growers live, as well as shared facilities including a barn and diesel generator, to cover any power not provided by the farm’s solar panels.
Gomersall’s farm, Cân y Pridd (Welsh for Song of the Soil), totals 4.9 hectares but she is now only growing on half a hectare, including in polytunnels, where she says she is “producing very big volumes for the scale”.


View image in fullscreen
Duncan Fisher, of Our Food Trust, which works to increase levels of homegrown produce. Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian
She and her two neighbours are already providing fresh fruit and vegetables for the local community, through a veg box subscription service and at markets. In late July, they also started supplying fresh produce to Birmingham city council, where it is distributed to holiday clubs, giving disadvantaged children a taste of homegrown veg for perhaps the first time.


The Wern farm project was launched by Our Food Trust, a charity which is working to increase levels of homegrown produce and aims to tackle Britain’s food insecurity.
The UK depends on imports for about 40% of its food and has one of the lowest food self-sufficiency ratios among large western European countries, leaving it exposed to supply shocks prompted by the climate crisis, or other risks including geopolitical tensions and cyber-attacks.
Just 0.2% of land in Wales is used for horticulture, according to the charity, giving huge scope for expansion. “We have to produce a lot more food for the regional and local market and for our cities,” says Duncan Fisher, joint chief executive at the charity.
One way to do this is to remove barriers for young people who want to get into growing, Fisher says, but who often find themselves priced out of renting or buying land and a suitable home. “There are lots of well-trained and skilful growers who can’t find land to grow food on,” he says. “The price of land here is set by the market, by people who are not going to farm it.”

I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.

So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.


View image in fullscreen
A jocotoco antpitta in the Tapichalaca reserve. Photograph: Javier Aznar González de Rueda

As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.

Plug-in solar panels, newly on the market in the UK, offer households a new way to cut down on their energy bills – but they don’t work for everyone.



Some housing associations have already banned renters from using the £700 plug-in devices over safety concerns, red tape around planning rules and uncertainty over responsibility if something goes wrong.



One manufacturer claims that there is an alternative option – shared solar panels.





How you could save £490 a year



Jack Taylor, general manager for Europe at Allume Energy, which manufactures shared solar panel and battery systems, claimed that one of his company’s systems – which distributes solar energy and battery storage – could cut each resident’s energy bill by up to £490 a year.



The estimated calculation is based on a recording of renters’ savings in Cardiff between July 2025 to June 2026 on a block of 24 flats.



But any savings made from shared solar panels will vary depending on the type of building, roof orientation, household consumption and energy tariffs of renters in a block of flats.

Champagne lovers may find themselves getting tipsy more quickly after French producers have been given the go-ahead to raise the alcohol content in a bottle of bubbly for the first time following this summer's record heatwave.
Winemakers can temporarily produce champagne with an alcohol content of up to 15% - above the 13% cap, industry officials have said.
The extreme heat and drought produced grapes with exceptionally higher sugar levels. Yeast converts sugar into alcohol during fermentation.
France's Champagne region also saw its earliest-ever harvest due to the weather, something that could become the norm "in 10 to 15 years" because of climate change, according to the Comite Champagne industry association.







How will extreme weather affect our food?





France links sharp rise in drownings to heatwaves
The temporary increase in champagne's alcohol content is only expected to affect a small number of wines, a spokeswoman for the Comite Champagne told the BBC.
During the second fermentation process, which gives champagne its bubbles, "a very small number of wines from this harvest could have slightly exceeded the regulatory limit of 13%, reaching around 13.1% or 13.2%". 
"Therefore a decision was made to exceptionally and temporarily increase the regulatory limit to 15% - only for this year," she said.

"The 2026 growing season will be remembered as one of the most unusual in Champagne's history, marked by severe spring frosts of historic intensity, an exceptionally early flowering period and five heatwaves throughout the summer." it added.

"The battle between what consumers want and what nature provides must be very stressful for producers."
The 2026 vintage is unlikely to hit shelves until 2028 as champagne must age for at least 15 months.

France has been one of Europe's worst-hit countries during this year's extreme weather, sparking huge wildfires.
